questions.stem: A student uses universal indicator to test four solutions and observes these colours: Solution P is red, Solution Q is green, Solution R is purple, Solution S is orange. Which solution is closest to neutral?

options.text: Solution P (red)
Solution Q (green)
Solution R (purple)
Solution S (orange)

questions.explanation: Universal indicator shows green at pH 7 (neutral). Red indicates a strong acid (pH 1-2), orange indicates a weak acid (pH 3-4), and purple indicates a strong alkali (pH 13-14). Solution Q (green) is closest to neutral with a pH of approximately 7.

questions.stem: A student performing a titration needs to determine the exact endpoint. Should she use universal indicator or phenolphthalein?

options.text: Universal indicator, because it gives more information about the pH
Phenolphthalein, because it gives a sharp colour change at a specific pH, making the endpoint easier to identify
Neither - indicators are not used in titrations
Universal indicator, because it changes colour at pH 7 exactly

questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein (or methyl orange) is preferred for titrations because it gives a sharp, distinct colour change at one specific pH. This makes the endpoint easy to identify precisely. Universal indicator gives a gradual colour change over a range of pH values, making it difficult to identify the exact endpoint.

questions.stem: Litmus paper turns red in an acidic solution. A student dips red litmus paper into a solution and it stays red. She concludes the solution must be acidic. Is she correct?

options.text: Yes, red litmus staying red proves the solution is acidic
No, red litmus stays red in both acidic and neutral solutions - she should also test with blue litmus
Yes, because litmus only works in acidic solutions
No, litmus is not a real indicator

questions.explanation: Red litmus stays red in both acidic AND neutral solutions. It only changes to blue in alkaline solutions. To confirm a solution is acidic, she should also test with blue litmus paper - if it turns red, the solution is acidic. Using both red and blue litmus together can distinguish acidic, neutral, and alkaline solutions.

questions.stem: Methyl orange is red below pH 3.1 and yellow above pH 4.4. Why would this indicator be suitable for a titration of a strong acid with a strong alkali?

options.text: Because it changes colour at exactly pH 7
Because the pH changes very rapidly near the endpoint of a strong acid-strong alkali titration, passing through pH 3.1-4.4 with just one drop
Because it only works with strong acids
Because yellow is easier to see than other colours

questions.explanation: In a strong acid-strong alkali titration, the pH changes very sharply near the equivalence point (jumping from about pH 3 to pH 11 with just one drop). Methyl orange's colour change range (3.1-4.4) falls within this sharp jump, so the colour change is sudden and distinct. The indicator does not need to change at exactly pH 7.

questions.stem: A student needs to test whether soil in a garden is acidic. She does not have a pH meter. Which method using indicators would give her the most useful information?

options.text: Add litmus paper directly to the soil
Mix the soil with distilled water, filter, then test the filtrate with universal indicator
Sprinkle phenolphthalein powder on the soil
Hold methyl orange paper above the soil

questions.explanation: The best approach is to mix soil with distilled water to dissolve any soluble acidic or alkaline substances, filter to get a clear solution, then test with universal indicator. This gives an approximate pH reading. Universal indicator is chosen over litmus because it shows the degree of acidity/alkalinity through a range of colours.
